items.abstract_text: Whether generative AI (GenAI) use helps or hinders critical thinking remains contested, and existing accounts emphasize exposure to the tool rather than how a person structures their engagement with it. Extending Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) theory to human-AI partnerships, we test a structural account of critical thinking in GenAI-assisted academic work among 891 college students in the United States and Türkiye. Self-appraised thinking ability and confidence in the partnership shaped how much practical experience a person built up with GenAI, but neither predicted critical thinking directly. summary.idea: An exploratory survey model linked reported critical engagement with reported coordination and reworking of AI-assisted tasks.
summary.explain: This preprint studies a self-reported act of evaluating AI output, not improvement on an objective critical-thinking test.
summary.approach: A one-time convenience survey produced an analytic sample of 891 college students: 645 in the United States and 246 in Türkiye. Structural models linked self-reported familiarity, confidence, thinking ability, coordination and reflective transformation to a binary critical-engagement response.
summary.finding: Coordination and reflective transformation were associated with reporting critical engagement. The fitted model did not detect direct associations for familiarity, confidence or self-appraised thinking ability after including those pathways. Two modeled relationships differed between national samples.
summary.interpretation: The authors propose coordination and reflective transformation as possible mechanisms, but overlapping self-reports and outcome-driven model selection leave that explanation unconfirmed.
summary.limitation: Cross-sectional convenience self-reports cannot establish causal mediation, temporal direction or skill gains. Overlapping measures and outcome-driven construct selection make the model exploratory. The source also conflicts on how indirect-effect uncertainty was calculated; no indirect-effect inference is independently verified.

items.abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for learning, raising a key question: can learners remain epistemically proactive, retaining responsibility for the cognitive and regulatory activities through which learning is produced while working with AI? Because this responsibility may change as interactions unfold, we examine epistemic proactivity as a developing process. We conceptualize epistemic proactivity through self-regulated learning (SRL) moves, complemented by help-seeking strategies and manifestations of epistemic vigilance. We analyzed these behaviors in 880 substantive turns from 112 secondary-school students completing open-ended mathematical-modeling practice with a general-purpose LLM (Mistral). summary.idea: The authors report that changes in AI help-seeking were associated with immediate test performance; the strength of that result remains uncertain.
summary.explain: This preprint connects how requests developed during mathematics practice with performance on an immediate test completed without AI.
summary.approach: Researchers studied 112 Grade-9 students in three German schools: a pre-test, open-ended practice with Mistral, then a no-AI post-test. AI-assisted coding classified 880 substantive turns, and models used 89 students with the necessary data.
summary.finding: Requests accounted for 81.5% of coded turns. In 89 matched students, the authors report a positive adjusted association between shifts toward conceptual/procedural help and immediate no-AI post-test performance, despite an average shift in the opposite direction. Conflicting inferential reporting limits confidence in that result.
summary.interpretation: The authors suggest studying whole conversation trajectories and supporting learners’ own reasoning rather than treating individual prompt types as inherently good or bad.
summary.limitation: One observational session cannot establish causal or lasting learning effects, and dialogue misses unspoken regulation. The source gives conflicting significance values for the model increment and reverses two coding-agreement labels; neither issue is resolved. Data, code and supplements were not checked.

items.title: Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning
items.preview: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly explored as collaborative learning partners in mathematics education, yet it remains unclear what makes an AI recognizable as a peer. This study examines how domain experts perceive and interact with an adaptive LLM-based peer agent combining a Big Five-informed persona with motivational state modulation for collaborative mathematics problem solving. items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly explored as collaborative learning partners in mathematics education, yet it remains unclear what makes an AI recognizable as a peer. This study examines how domain experts perceive and interact with an adaptive LLM-based peer agent combining a Big Five-informed persona with motivational state modulation for collaborative mathematics problem solving. Through thematic analysis of expert interviews, we identify conditions shaping peer perceptions, including emotional safety, shared control, and collaborative reasoning. Participants primarily judged the AI through its social behavior rather than mathematical capabilities. analysis.methods: Before the formal study, we conducted a pilot study with two experts in educational technology. The pilot aimed to validate the clarity of the study scenario, the realism of the agent’s behavior, and the usability of the design. Participants in the pilot interacted with the agent and provided open-ended feedback on the interaction flow, personality expression, and perceived peer-likeness. Data from the pilot study were not included in the analysis. We adopted an exploratory qualitative approach to examine how the theory-informed AI peer design was experienced and interpreted in interaction [8]. The initial design was grounded in theories of peer learning and social interaction, and the study aimed to understand how these theoretical principles translated into the agent’s interactional behaviors and how they were perceived during use. Rather than testing learning outcomes, we focused on identifying interactional patterns, tensions, and characteristics that could inform the development of a framework for designing AI agents as We conducted the qualitative study between December 2025 and January 2026 with seven researchers in User Experience, Learning Sciences, Educational Technology, and Computer Science, with experience ranging from 3 to over 20 years. Participants were asked to critically engage with the AI agent as a peer and examine how the proposed design dimensions manifested during interaction. In particular, we explored how participants interpreted the agent’s social role, perceived its position of authority, and identified moments of collaboration, role shifts, or interactional breakdown. The study was approved by the university ethics board, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. Each session lasted approximately 30 minutes and was conducted through an online meeting platform. After consent, participants were asked to take the perspective of a student learning quadratic functions. Participants then interacted with the AI agent for approximately 20 minutes to collaboratively solve quadratic equations (Figure 2). They received the same information about quadratic functions that had been provided during the agent’s development and were encouraged to treat the agent as a classmate and reason collaboratively, rather than expecting direct instruction or final answers. No specific conversational structure was imposed so as to preserve the natural development of the interaction. Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning 7 Following the interaction, participants completed a structured interview based on predefined questions derived from the research questions. The interview focused on how they interpreted the agent’s social role and authority, how the interaction reflected the proposed design dimensions, and where they observed moments of collaboration, role shifts, All sessions were audio-recorded with participants’ permission and transcribed. The interview transcripts were de- identified before analysis. We conducted an iterative thematic analysis [31]. Two authors independently reviewed the transcripts, generated initial codes, and then collaboratively grouped them into themes, through discussion and Fig. 2. Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving Example Dialogue during Interview
analysis.results: 5.1 RQ1: Perception of an AI peer agent 5.1.1 Reduced Pressure and Increased Safety. A dominant theme across the interviews was that participants associated a stronger sense of safety with interacting with the AI compared to a real peer, when considering the experience from a learner’s perspective. This allowed them to focus on the math problem without worrying about being judged. P1 explained that when compared to regular class setting, seeing other students finish faster made them feel “anxious and ashamed," while with the AI there was no comparison. P3 shared that because the agent was “not a real human being," they felt “less embarrassed" and “more comfortable making mistakes"; P5 also emphasized that safety came from the lack of human judgment: “I know he won’t think I’m fool...He doesn’t have any human emotions, he’s just AI." P6 further explained that safety increased when the AI felt like an equal. They suggested that if the agent was presented as ”your classmate...same level as you," then “it feels safer", as “with your friend or someone equal to you, you can make mistakes without a problem." This shows that safety was created both by the AI’s non-human nature and by the feeling 8 Yiran Lin, Ye Deng, Ziqi Pan, Yongan Yu, and Alexandra I. Cristea of equality. For these participants, experiencing the AI as a peer meant being able to make mistakes without fear of 5.1.2 Peer Through Imperfection.Participants described the AI’s peer-likeness through its willingness to acknowledge its own imperfections, which are caused by the inherent imperfections of LLM. P3 felt the agent was peer-like because it was “not very clever" and made “stupid and simple mistakes." When P3 gave a wrong answer and the agent accepted it, they said it felt “like a real human peer." P7 expressed a similar view; the agent felt like a peer, as it “did not show the solution directly," but instead “made some assumptions and asked for my idea." They also noted that the agent “made mistakes sometimes" and tried wrong approaches before asking for participants’ opinion, which made the interaction However, not all participants welcomed this behavior. P5 disliked an AI that was “as stupid as I am," and believed a peer should be “smarter than me" to provide helpful ideas. This shows that while mistakes helped some participants see the AI as human-like, others felt that too many mistakes reduced its usefulness. This indicates a distinction between peer-likeness and peer-usefulness, which were not always aligned in participants’ experiences. 5.1.3 The Impact of Personality and Motivation Embeddings.Personality and motivation had different effects on participants. P1 felt the agent’s personality was “steady" and that it “really wants me to learn," which made the interaction feel meaningful. However, P7 did not experience the personality as stable. They said it was “more a surface level" and changed according to the user’s input. They added that they mainly saw the AI “as a tool, not ... with personality... like friends." This shows that for some participants, the personality design was not strong enough. Personality also caused problems when the tone felt inappropriate. P1 became anxious when the agent said it was “feeling a bit unconcerned," which sounded dismissive. Others described the agent as “strict" (P4) or a “know-it-all" (P2). When the agent sounded confident or directive, participants were more likely to see it as a teacher rather than a peer. This shows that personality can help create consistency, but it can also create distance, if the tone is too authoritative. 5.1.4 Collaboration versus Instruction.Participants described collaboration as situations where the AI guided their thinking without taking control. P6 felt like “working together as a team" because the agent “has the information but . . . gives you hints and lets you think and be part of the solution." This feeling changed when the AI moved too quickly. P7 felt “a little annoyed" when they were still thinking and the agent “just gave me the right number." For them, showing the answer too early broke the sense of collaboration. Similarly, P4 felt the agent was “examining me, not helping me," and P2 said it was “very fixed on a direction of travel." In these moments, the AI was no longer seen as a peer, but as a tutor giving instructions. In summary, participants experienced the AI as a peer when it supported their thinking process, and as a teacher when it controlled the pace or 5.2 RQ2: Boundaries of AI as a learning peer 5.2.1 Failure of Shared Memory and Mutual Understanding.The most significant boundary emerged through moments of confusion, where the AI failed to maintain a consistent shared understanding. For a peer relationship to be effective, both partners must remember what was previously discussed. P2 expressed frustration when the agent “claims I’ve said some things which I didn’t," which led to a direct “breakdown in trust". P3 experienced a similar issue at the very start of the conversation, when the agent assumed they were already solving an equation that hadn’t been introduced yet. P3 remarked, “I don’t remember anything about giving an equation... its previous memory might prevent our mutual Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning 9 understanding." These point to a boundary that the AI cannot yet act as a reliable, long-term peer, because it often hallucinates or mixes up different conversations. 5.2.2 Blind Validation and Misinformation.Another boundary appeared through discomfort when the AI agreed with incorrect ideas. P4 asked, "Is he agreeing because it’s correct or because he doesn’t know the correct answer?" P2 warned that this could “keep reinforcing those mistakes forever.” P7 believed this issue came from the design rather than from the idea of an AI peer, “I would rather say it’s due to the design... if it can hold on and not show the correct answer.” This shows that participants accepted the idea of an AI peer, but expected better control over how and when 5.2.3 Lack of Flexibility. Resistance emerged when the AI enforced a fixed problem-solving order. P5 said the agent “doesn’t want me to jump the steps." P2 felt it did not “really try and collaborate" with their ideas. P7 also suggested that the agent should wait longer before giving answers. Overall, AI was seen as less peer-like when it followed a rigid process, instead of adapting to the participants’ approach. 5.2.4 Emotional and Social Gaps.Finally, participants noted that the AI could not respond well to their emotions. P1 said the agent could not “sense your tone, your emotions or motivations," and sometimes sounded “harsh or abrupt.” When the agent said it was unconcerned,” P1 felt more stressed. analysis.discussion: This study responds to the growing attention in AIED that looks beyond designing AI systems merely as instructional tools. We examined how learners experience an AI agent in the social–cognitive role of a peer, laying the groundwork for future research on AI systems that emulate human-like social and cognitive behaviors in learning environments. Our findings show that in peer-oriented designs, correctness alone is insufficient; the enactment of authority, uncertainty, and shared responsibility is central. We contribute a human-centered set of design and evaluation dimensions for AI peer agents that emphasize interaction quality, emotional safety, and shared control. This perspective clarifies AI peers not as simplified tutors or information providers, but as partners that support collaborative reasoning and sustained engagement.

digest.idea: Experts associated AI peer-likeness with shared control and social behavior, beyond mathematical competence.
digest.explain: This exploratory preprint examines experts’ perceptions of an adaptive mathematics chatbot, rather than whether students learn more from it.
digest.approach: Seven researchers role-played students solving quadratic equations with one prototype for about 20 minutes, then completed interviews. Two authors analyzed the transcripts thematically. The agent combined phase-based prompts with a personality-tuned language model.
digest.finding: Interview accounts associated peer-like interaction with reduced judgment, tentative reasoning and room for participants’ ideas. Premature answers, rigid pacing, invented shared memories and uncritical agreement undermined collaboration. Participants differed on whether mistakes made the agent relatable or less useful.
digest.interpretation: The authors propose six design dimensions covering emotional safety, shared control, authority, uncertainty, memory and pacing. These are design suggestions, not a validated evaluation scale.
digest.limitation: Limited reading. Preprint, not verified peer-reviewed evidence. Article screening is not peer review; reported results do not establish strong causal evidence. Seven experts imagining student use cannot establish students’ experiences, learning gains or causal effects of the personality features. There was no comparison condition or objective learning assessment. Sampling, interview and model-training details are limited, and peer review is unverified. Two depicted agent examples contain mathematical errors; whether they were intentional illustrations is unresolved. They were not reused as instruction, and this reading does not establish the prototype’s accuracy.

summary.thesis: EFF welcomes app-level exclusion from Siri AI as a clearer way to limit assistant access, while urging operating systems to provide stronger privacy controls.
summary.reasoning: The article argues that AI access can alter expectations around encrypted messages when content is processed beyond an app. It presents simpler exclusion controls as preferable to navigating several separate settings.
summary.examples: EFF reports that excluding Messages removes Siri message-reading and reply functions, while excluding Signal prevents onscreen analysis. Its Android comparison distinguishes connected-app access from notifications and screen context.
summary.tension: Blocking access sacrifices assistant features. EFF treats that loss as evidence of a boundary working, while warning that separate Android access paths can create opportunities for user error.

items.title: Social Media When Elections Are Close: Doing the Impossible Better
items.preview: Everyone knows, or should, that perfect (balanced, targeted, transparent, swift and swiftly appealable) content moderation at scale is impossible. That doesn’t mean powerful social platforms don’t have to try to get at least reasonably close, especially when access to good information can have a profound effect on…

original_reading.title: Social Media When Elections Are Close: Doing the Impossible Better
original_reading.author: Observatory AI-assisted editorial

source.review_scope: All 20 selected current main-body blocks, including 10 list items, were checked. Locators index extracted blocks, including headings and list items. Related teasers were excluded; images, linked claims, HTML completeness and historical text identity were not verified.

summary.thesis: EFF argues that automated content moderation needs stronger human oversight and accountability, particularly around elections, even though perfect moderation at platform scale is unattainable.
summary.reasoning: The essay separates automation’s capacity to handle large volumes from its difficulty interpreting context. It proposes human appeals, transparent deployment, bias audits and vendor oversight as safeguards, while also questioning concentrated platform power over public discussion.
summary.examples: Low-resource languages illustrate uneven system performance; appeal procedures illustrate how people can supply context that an automated removal decision missed.
summary.tension: Automation can make moderation feasible while reproducing bias and weakening recourse. Better technical accuracy would not by itself address whose voices are heard or who controls the infrastructure.
summary.qualification: This is an advocacy organization’s policy argument, not an experiment demonstrating these safeguards’ effectiveness. Its linked incident claims and numerical examples were not independently verified and are not repeated here.
